# std/io

Stdin/stdout and owned file handles. (Read-by-path helpers — `readFile`, `readLines`,
`splitLines` — live in [`std/fs`](fs).)

```milo
from "std/io" import { File, readLine, writeStdout }
```

## Example

Count the lines on stdin, then write to a file:

```milo
var n = 0
while let Option.Some(_) = readLine() {
    n += 1
}
var f = File.openWrite("count.txt")!
let _ = f.writeAll($"{n}\n")
```

## API reference

### `BufReader`

```milo
pub struct BufReader<R: Reader>
```

Buffered reads over any Reader, and the reason the Reader trait exists: without
it `readByte` is one read(2) per byte.

It OWNS the source. `BufReader<File>.new(f)` consumes the File and closes it on
drop; `BufReader<FdStream>.new(sock.stream())` borrows the descriptor instead and
leaves the socket writable. Spell the type argument — a bare `BufReader.new(f)`
does not resolve on a generic struct today.

Fields: `inner: R`, `buf: string`, `pos: i64`, `cap: i64`, `ended: bool`.


#### `BufReader.readLine`

```milo
fn BufReader.readLine(self: &mut BufReader): Result<Option<string>, IoError>
```

One line without its terminator. Strips a trailing CR so CRLF input reads the
same as LF input. None at end of stream — the `while let` loop condition.

#### `BufReader.readUntil`

```milo
fn BufReader.readUntil(self: &mut BufReader, delim: u8): Result<Option<string>, IoError>
```

Bytes up to (and consuming) `delim`, with the delimiter itself stripped.
None means the stream was already at its end; a final unterminated run comes
back as Some, so no input is ever silently discarded.

### `BufWriter`

```milo
pub struct BufWriter<W: Writer>
```

Buffered writes over any Writer, collapsing many small writes into one.

**Unflushed bytes are not lost if you forget to flush**: drop flushes. If that
last flush fails there is nowhere to return the error to, so it goes to stderr
rather than vanishing. Call `flush()` explicitly wherever a write error is
something your program can act on — that is the only way to *handle* one.

There is deliberately no `intoInner()`: a struct with a Drop impl cannot have a
field moved out of it, and giving up flush-on-drop to buy one back would be the
wrong trade.

Fields: `inner: W`, `buf: string`, `cap: i64`.


### `FdReader`

```milo
pub enum FdReader
```

A read cursor over a raw fd whose read strategy is fixed at construction:
under the green scheduler it parks the task on the event loop at EAGAIN; on a
plain OS thread it blocks in the kernel. attach() decides once from runtime
truth and welds that choice to the fd's O_NONBLOCK state, so no caller ever
threads an "in green?" flag — the sharp edge where a wrong bool either stalls
the whole cooperative runtime (a blocking read inside a green task) or spins
treating EAGAIN as EOF (parking with no scheduler). Illegal states are
unrepresentable: a Green reader implies a non-blocking fd, a Blocking one a
blocking read path.

The reader borrows the fd; it does not own or close it. Keep the owning
source (File / Pty / Child / socket) alive for the reader's lifetime.

Variants:

- `Green(i32)`
- `Blocking(i32)`

#### `FdReader.readByte`

```milo
fn FdReader.readByte(self: &FdReader): i64
```

Read one byte, returned as 0..255. Returns -1 at EOF or on error.

#### `FdReader.readExact`

```milo
fn FdReader.readExact(self: &FdReader, n: i64): Result<string>
```

Read exactly n bytes into a string. Err if the stream ends first.

### `FdStream`

```milo
pub struct FdStream
```

A borrowed byte stream over an OS handle — the adapter that turns anything with
a descriptor (file, socket, pipe, pty, child stdio) into a Reader and a Writer.

It does NOT own the handle and will never close it. Keep the owning value (File,
TcpStream, Pty, Child) alive and open for as long as the stream is in use; this
is the same rule `FdReader` and `fdChannel` already carry, and it is what makes
a simultaneous BufReader and BufWriter on one socket expressible at all.

The compiler cannot check that rule — a descriptor number is an integer, not a
reference — so this is the one sharp edge in the streams API:

    BufReader&lt;FdStream>.new(File.openRead(p)!.stream())   // WRONG: the File is a
                                                          // temporary and closes
                                                          // at the end of the line
    var f = File.openRead(p)!                             // right: the handle has
    BufReader&lt;FdStream>.new(f.stream())                   // a name and outlives it

When you do not need the handle back, do not use a view at all: `File` implements
Reader and Writer itself, so `BufReader<File>.new(f)` takes ownership and the
question cannot arise.

Fields: `fd: i32`, `socket: bool`.

```milo

```

Writes here go straight at fd 1, bypassing the stdio buffer `print` uses, so
the two interleave in the wrong order. Pick one per output session — that is
why this does not fflush on your behalf: doing so per write would defeat the
buffering you wrapped it in a BufWriter to get.

#### `File.close`

```milo
fn File.close(self: &mut File): Result<Unit, IoError>
```

Close now instead of at drop, and report failure. Drop closes silently, which
is fine for reads but hides a write error that only surfaces at close (NFS,
full filesystems). After this the File is inert and its drop is a no-op.

```milo

```

Move the read/write cursor to an absolute byte offset. Returns the new
offset. A BufReader over this file caches bytes past its own cursor, so
seeking underneath one desynchronizes it — seek first, then wrap.


Size of the open file in bytes. The read position is left where it was.

#### `File.stream`

```milo

```

A non-owning Reader+Writer view of this file, for when the File itself must
stay put (e.g. you want a BufReader and a BufWriter on the same handle).
The File must outlive the view and the compiler does not check that — see
FdStream. Prefer `BufReader<File>.new(f)`, which owns the handle outright.

### `IoError`

```milo
pub enum IoError
```

Why an I/O operation failed. The four named variants carry the path; `Other` carries
a message (from a path operation, the path plus the OS reason).

Variants:

- `NotFound(string)`
- `PermissionDenied(string)`
- `IsDirectory(string)`
- `AlreadyExists(string)`
- `Other(string)`

### `Reader`

```milo
pub trait Reader
```

The two byte-stream interfaces every source and sink in std composes against.

They are *traits*, not `interface`s, and that is forced by the language rather
than chosen for speed: an `interface` value is a fat pointer that has to live
somewhere, and Milo references are second-class, so a stored `&Reader` cannot
exist. A trait is monomorphized into the holder — `BufReader<File>` is a real
struct containing a real `File` — which means the wrapper *owns* its source and
no lifetime ever escapes. The cost is that a `Vec<Reader>` of mixed sources is
not expressible; wrap the mixed case in an enum of concrete sources instead.

Both use `IoError`. That is not a claim that every module's errors are unified
(they are not) — it is that a read or a write on a byte stream fails for kernel
reasons, and `IoError` is the enum that already carries them.

#### `Reader.read`

```milo
fn Reader.read(self: &mut Reader, max: i64): Result<string, IoError>
```

### Functions

#### `copyStream`

```milo
pub fn copyStream<R: Reader, W: Writer>(src: &mut R, dst: &mut W): Result<i64, IoError>
```

Drain `src` into `dst`, returning the byte count. The pipe that makes any source
usable with any sink. Does NOT flush `dst` — a caller stacking more onto the same
writer should not pay for a flush per copy.

#### `defaultBufferSize`

```milo
pub fn defaultBufferSize(): i64
```

Default buffer size for BufReader/BufWriter. Big enough that per-byte and
per-line work amortizes to roughly one syscall per 64 KiB.

#### `fdChannel`

```milo
pub fn fdChannel(fd: i32): Channel<string>
```

Stream a file descriptor's bytes on a background green task, returned as a
channel of raw chunks. This is the single pump behind every async byte source
(pty, sockets, child stdio, pipes) — the caller just `recv`s or iterates
(`for chunk in fdChannel(fd)`), never touching read/EAGAIN. The channel closes
at EOF (read returns &lt;= 0). Milo's answer to a node.js Readable, minus the fd.

LIFETIME: the detached pump holds the raw fd. Keep the owning source (Pty /
TcpStream / Child) alive and open for as long as you consume the channel —
closing or dropping it out from under the pump strands the pump (parks
forever), and for a TLS source would read freed SSL state.

#### `fdReaderAttach`

```milo
pub fn fdReaderAttach(fd: i32): FdReader
```

Capture the read strategy from the current runtime context, flipping the fd
non-blocking iff we will park on it so the two never drift apart. Free fn (not
an FdReader method) because milo resolves `FdReader.attach` as a variant, not
a static method.


map errno to IoError variant with path context

#### `putChar`

```milo
pub fn putChar(ch: u8): void
```

Write a single byte to stdout.

Goes onto the same stdio buffer `print` writes to — one syscall per byte would be
absurd for a per-character API, and a raw fd write would also land ahead of any
buffered `print` output.

#### `readLine`

```milo
pub fn readLine(): Option<string>
```

Read a single line from stdin. Returns None at EOF.

#### `readStdin`

```milo
pub fn readStdin(): string
```

Read all of stdin into a string (blocks to EOF). Prefer `stdinChannel()` for
streaming/incremental consumption.

#### `stdinChannel`

```milo
pub fn stdinChannel(): Channel<string>
```

Stream stdin as an iterable channel of chunks — the async counterpart to the
blocking readStdin/readLine. `for chunk in stdinChannel() { ... }`.
NOTE: this puts fd 0 into O_NONBLOCK and does not restore it, so afterward the
blocking readLine/readStdin on the same tty may return early. Pick one style
per stdin session; don't mix streaming and blocking reads of the same fd.

#### `writeStdout`

```milo
pub fn writeStdout(s: &string): void
```

Write a string to stdout without appending a newline.

`print` goes through stdio's buffer; this goes straight at the fd. Drain the
buffer first or the two interleave in the wrong order. fflush on an already-empty
buffer is not a syscall, so a program that only ever uses this pays nothing.
